# dcb_layer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dcb-layer/0.2.1/dcb_layer/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#dcb)dcb

A [DCB-compliant](https://dcb.events) event store backed by [FoundationDB](https://www.foundationdb.org).

Events are appended atomically, assigned a globally ordered [ Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html) position,
and indexed for fast retrieval by type, tags, or both.
Optimistic concurrency is enforced through

[s that fail the write if matching events appeared since the caller last read.](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html)

`AppendCondition`[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use dcb_layer::{Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Open a FoundationDB database (see foundationdb-rs for setup).
    let _network = unsafe { foundationdb::boot() };
    let db = foundationdb::Database::default().unwrap();
    // 2. Create a namespaced store — namespace isolates data within one FDB cluster.
    let store = FdbStore::new(db, "my-app");
    // 3. Append events (no condition = unconditional write).
    let event = Event::new(
        "OrderPlaced",
        ["order:42", "customer:7"],
        b"{\"total\":99}".as_slice(),
    );
    let position = store.append(vec![event], vec![]).await.unwrap();
    // 4. Read events back — filter by type, tags, or both.
    let results = store
        .read(
            Query {
                items: vec![QueryItem {
                    types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
                    tags: vec!["customer:7".into()],
                }],
            },
            None,
        )
        .await
        .unwrap();
    println!("Found {} event(s), first at {:?}", results.len(), results[0].position);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core concepts

[§](https://docs.rs#event)Event

An [ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) carries three fields, constructed via

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html#method.new)

`Event::new`| Field | Accepts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `type_name` | `&str`/`String` | Required, non-empty (e.g. `"OrderPlaced"`) |
| `tags` | any iterable of strings | Up to 10 tags; `"_"`is reserved |
| `data` | `&[u8]`/`Vec<u8>` | Opaque bytes — encode however you like |

Tags are free-form strings. A common convention is `"entity:id"` (e.g. `"order:42"`),
but the store treats them as opaque labels.

[§](https://docs.rs#query)Query

A [ Query](https://docs.rs/struct.Query.html) is a list of

[s joined by](https://docs.rs/struct.QueryItem.html)

`QueryItem`**OR**. Each item matches events that satisfy

**all**of its constraints:

- `types`— event’s- `type_name`must be one of these (empty = any type)
- `tags`— event must carry- **all**of these tags (empty = any tags)

Every item must specify at least one type or one tag.

```
use dcb_layer::{Query, QueryItem};
// Match OrderPlaced OR OrderCancelled events tagged with order:42
let query = Query {
    items: vec![
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderCancelled".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
    ],
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#appendcondition)AppendCondition

An [ AppendCondition](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html) guards a write with an optimistic-concurrency check:
the

`append` call fails with [if any event matching](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.AppendConditionFailed)

`Error::AppendConditionFailed``query` exists **after**the

`after` position (or at all, when `after` is `None`).The typical pattern:

- Read events matching your query → note the last position seen.
- Build your decision model from those events.
- Append new events with `after = last_position`to guard against concurrent writes.

```
use dcb_layer::{AppendCondition, Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
// 1. Read events and note the last position seen.
let results = store.read(
    Query { items: vec![QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] }] },
    None,
).await.unwrap();
let last_position = results.last().map(|e| e.position);
// 2. Append new events — fail if a concurrent write snuck in after last_position.
let condition = AppendCondition {
    query: Query {
        items: vec![QueryItem {
            types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
            tags: vec!["order:42".into()],
        }],
    },
    after: last_position,
};
store.append(vec![Event::new("OrderPlaced", ["order:42"], b"".as_slice())], vec![condition]).await.unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#readoptions)ReadOptions

[ ReadOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadOptions.html) controls pagination and ordering:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | `0`(unlimited) | Maximum events to return |
| `after` | `None` | Only return events after this position |
| `reverse` | `false` | Newest-first when `true` |

[§](https://docs.rs#limits)Limits

| Constraint | Value |
|---|---|
| Max events per `append`call | 65 535 |
| Max tags per event | 10 |
| Reserved tag value | `"_"` |

[§](https://docs.rs#practical-sizing)Practical sizing

Each event writes one index key per **subset** of its tags (2^n keys for
n tags — up to 1 024 for 10 tags). All writes of an `append` call share one
FDB transaction, which is capped at 10 MB of affected data and 5 seconds —
keep batches small when events carry many tags.

Reads run in a single FDB transaction too: an unbounded [ FdbStore::read](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read)
or

[over a large store fails with](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read_all)

`FdbStore::read_all``transaction_too_old` (FDB error 1007) after a bounded number of retries.
Paginate with

`ReadOptions``limit` + `after`.Subscription cursors ([ FdbStore::set_cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.set_cursor)) are last-writer-wins; run
one consumer per cursor name or coordinate externally.

[§](https://docs.rs#foundationdb-setup)FoundationDB setup

This crate wraps the [ foundationdb](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) crate.
You are responsible for:

- installing and running an FDB cluster
- calling `unsafe { foundationdb::boot() }`once at startup (keeps the network thread alive)
- opening a `foundationdb::Database``FdbStore::new`

Refer to the [foundationdb-rs documentation](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) and
the [FoundationDB developer guide](https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/getting-started-linux.html)
for cluster setup and client configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#fdb-api-version)FDB API version

The default Cargo feature targets FDB 7.4. To use FDB 7.3, disable the default features:

`dcb-layer = { version = "...", default-features = false, features = ["fdb-7_3"] }`The feature selects the C API headers compiled against; a newer `libfdb_c` is backward compatible.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html)
- 12-byte globally unique, monotonically increasing position. Bytes 0–9: FDB transaction version (big-endian). Bytes 10–11: user version = batch index (big-endian u16).

# hdf5_metno - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hdf5-metno/0.13.0/hdf5_metno/

## Expand description

HDF5 for Rust.

This crate provides thread-safe Rust bindings and high-level wrappers for the `HDF5`
library API. Some of the features include:

- Thread-safety with non-threadsafe libhdf5 builds guaranteed via reentrant mutexes.
- Native representation of most HDF5 types, including variable-length strings and arrays.
- Derive-macro for automatic mapping of user structs and enums to `HDF5`types.
- Multi-dimensional array reading/writing interface via `ndarray`.

Direct low-level bindings are also available and provided in the `hdf5-sys` crate.

Requires `HDF5` library of version 1.8.4 or later. Newer versions will enable additional
features of the library. Such items are marked in the documentation with a version number
indicating the required version of `HDF5`. The `have-direct` and `have-parallel` features
also indicates `HDF5` functionality.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [dataset](https://docs.rs/dataset/index.html)
- Multi-dimensional datasets.
- [datatype](https://docs.rs/datatype/index.html)
- Datatype objects for defining the layout of a data element.
- [file](https://docs.rs/file/index.html)
- HDF5 file objects.
- [filters](https://docs.rs/filters/index.html)
- Filters for data compression and validation during file I/O.
- [plist](https://docs.rs/plist/index.html)
- Property list objects.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)
- Base types and interfaces for creating compound data types.

# swarm_abm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/swarm-abm/0.3.0/swarm_abm/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#swarm-abm)swarm-abm

Spatial agent-based modeling (ABM) engine: agents on a 2D grid, configurable scheduling, time-series data collection, and deterministic reproducibility (same seed → same results).

[§](https://docs.rs#concepts)Concepts

- `Agent`
- `Model`
- `Grid2D`
- `Schedule`- `decide`with an immutable model +- `apply`).
- `DataCollector`
- `Simulation`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-random-walkers)Example: random walkers

```
use swarm_abm::prelude::*;
struct Walker {
    pos: Pos,
}
struct World {
    agents: AgentSet<Walker>,
    visits: Grid2D<u32>,
}
impl Agent for Walker {
    type Model = World;
    fn step(&mut self, _id: AgentId, world: &mut World, rng: &mut SimRng) {
        if let Some(dest) =
            world.visits.random_neighbor(self.pos, Neighborhood::Moore, rng)
        {
            self.pos = dest;
            world.visits[self.pos] += 1;
        }
    }
}
impl Model for World {
    type Agent = Walker;
    fn agents(&self) -> &AgentSet<Walker> {
        &self.agents
    }
    fn agents_mut(&mut self) -> &mut AgentSet<Walker> {
        &mut self.agents
    }
}
let mut agents = AgentSet::new();
agents.insert(Walker { pos: Pos::new(5, 5) });
let visits = Grid2D::new(10, 10).with_torus(true);
let mut sim = Simulation::new(World { agents, visits }, 42);
sim.add_reporter("total_visits", |w: &World| {
    w.visits.iter().map(|(_, &v)| f64::from(v)).sum()
});
sim.run(100);
assert_eq!(sim.step_count(), 100);
assert_eq!(sim.data().series("total_visits").unwrap().last(), Some(&100.0));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [agent](https://docs.rs/agent/index.html)
- `Agent`- `AgentSet`
- [batch](https://docs.rs/batch/index.html)
- Running **ensembles**and**parameter sweeps**.
- [continuous](https://docs.rs/continuous/index.html)
- **Continuous**2D space for off-lattice ABMs: movement,- *flocking*, particles — where position is real-valued (- `f64`), not a cell.
- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Per-step (`DataCollector``AgentDataCollector`
- [graph](https://docs.rs/graph/index.html)
- **Network**(graph) space for network ABMs: contagion on social networks, propagation in infrastructure, information diffusion, mobility.
- [grid](https://docs.rs/grid/index.html)
- Dense 2D grid with Moore and Von Neumann neighborhoods.
- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- `Model`
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports the types needed to define and run a model.
- [rng](https://docs.rs/rng/index.html)
- Seedable, deterministic random number generation.
- [schedule](https://docs.rs/schedule/index.html)
- Activation order of agents at each step.
- [sim](https://docs.rs/sim/index.html)
- Runner for the simulation: `Simulation`

# capsudod-pwauth 0.1.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capsudod-pwauth/0.1.2

# capsudo-rs

`sudo`, but [object-capability style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-capability_model) — a Rust reimplementation of
[capsudo](https://github.com/kaniini/capsudo) built so the capability channel
can be **proxied across  Edera Protect zones over IDM**, not just a
local Unix socket.

## The idea

Privilege is not granted by a setuid bit. A privileged daemon (`capsudod`) is
started ahead of time, already holding the privilege you want to delegate, and
bound to a *transport endpoint*. Whoever can reach that endpoint can invoke the
capability. The endpoint **is** the capability.

In the original, the endpoint is always an `AF_UNIX` socket whose file
permissions decide who may connect. Here the transport is abstracted: the same
protocol and the same client/daemon logic run unchanged over a local Unix
socket *or* a cross-zone IDM channel, so a capability held in one Edera zone can
be exposed to another without either side knowing the difference.

## What this enables

The motivating deployment is autonomous AI agents. An agent is sandboxed precisely because what it runs cannot be fully trusted, yet real work needs a few privileged operations: push this image, run that deploy script, restart a wedged service. The conventional escapes all grant ambient, stealable authority. A kubeconfig or SSH key mounted into the sandbox works from anywhere once exfiltrated, and sudo inside the sandbox puts privilege in the one place most likely to be prompt-injected.

capsudo restates the problem in object-capability terms. The agent's zone
holds no credentials at all; it holds an endpoint, and reaching the endpoint
is the permission. The daemon side fixes the command and environment (`-f`,
`-E`), so even a fully compromised client can only cause the pre-approved
operation to run. There is nothing to steal: the endpoint does not exist
outside the zone it was granted to, and its effect cannot be broadened from
the client side.

For the caller nothing changes: prefix a command, keep ordinary
stdin/stdout/stderr, exit codes, and fully interactive ptys, whether the
daemon is local or in another zone. In an Edera Protect deployment the grants
are declarative: the zone agent launches and manages the attenuated `capsudod`
instances from configuration and proxies an endpoint like `/run/cap/<name>`
into each authorized zone over IDM.

## Why a rewrite was needed for cross-zone

Two things in the original assume a shared kernel:

-
**Descriptor passing.**The caller's stdin/stdout/stderr are handed to the daemon over`SCM_RIGHTS`. File descriptors are meaningless across a zone boundary. Here the transport layer papers over that — real`SCM_RIGHTS`locally,**simulated**descriptor passing (stream multiplexing + local pipe ends) cross-zone — transparently, so client and daemon never learn which happened.
-
**The interactive pty.**The original allocates the pty on the*client*and ships the slave. A pty slave is a real terminal; a socket pair (all a cross-zone link can fabricate) is not. So the pty is allocated on the**daemon**side instead: the child always gets a genuine controlling terminal in its own zone, and only a byte stream plus window-size updates cross the channel. (The C version was updated to match.)

## Workspace layout

| Crate | Role |
|---|---|
| `capsudo-proto` | Transport-agnostic wire protocol: message types, portable fixed-endianness framing. No I/O. |
| `capsudo-transport` | `Transport`/`Listener`traits + implementations:`unix`(real`SCM_RIGHTS`),`mux`(simulated fd-passing over any byte channel),`fakeidm`(throwaway TCP cross-zone stub, feature`fakeidm`). |
| `capsudo-core` | Client and daemon session logic, written entirely against the traits. |
| `capsudo` | Client binary. |
| `capsudod` | Daemon binary (listening, or one-shot on stdin). |
| `capsudod-pwauth` | Authenticating front-end: shadow-password check, then chain to `capsudod`. Local sockets only: it identifies the caller via`SO_PEERCRED`, which does not exist across zones. |

## Build & test

```
cargo build
cargo test
cargo build --features capsudo-transport/fakeidm    # include the fake IDM stub
```
## Command-line

```
# Delegate "run anything" to whoever can reach the socket:
capsudod -S /run/capsudo/sudo -o root:wheel -m 0770 &
capsudo  -S /run/capsudo/sudo -- id
# Pin an exact command (client args ignored):
capsudod -S /run/capsudo/reboot -f /sbin/reboot &
capsudo  -S /run/capsudo/reboot
# Require a password first, then chain to capsudod:
capsudod-pwauth -S /run/capsudo/auth -o root:wheel -m 0770 -- capsudod &
capsudo -S /run/capsudo/auth -- id
```
See `CLAUDE.md` for the architecture in depth.

# capsudo_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capsudo-core/0.1.2/capsudo_core/

## Expand description

Client and daemon session logic for capsudo, generic over any
[ Transport](https://docs.rs/capsudo-transport/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capsudo_transport/traits/trait.Transport.html).

This crate contains the actual capsudo behaviour — the configuration handshake, attenuation policy, and program execution — with no knowledge of whether it is talking over a local Unix socket or a cross-zone IDM channel.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientRequest.html)- Request
- What the client is asking the daemon to do.
- [Daemon](https://docs.rs/struct.DaemonConfig.html)- Config
- Daemon-side policy applied to every session.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Core](https://docs.rs/enum.CoreError.html)- Error
- Errors arising from the client or daemon session logic.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/enum.SessionOutcome.html)- Outcome
- How a client session ended.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_winsize.html)- winsize
- Reads the current terminal dimensions from `fd`.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_client.html)- client
- Runs a client session to completion and returns the target program’s exit
status. Treats an authentication challenge as an error; use `run_session`
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_session.html)- session
- Runs one client session, optionally presenting `secret`for authentication.
- [serve_](https://docs.rs/fn.serve_connection.html)- connection
- Serves a single client connection: receives configuration, runs the program, and reports the exit status.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Convenience result alias for core operations.

capsudo -S /run/capsudo/auth -- id
```
See `CLAUDE.md` for the architecture in depth.

# capsudo_transport - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capsudo-transport/0.1.2/capsudo_transport/

## Expand description

Transport abstraction for capsudo.

The capsudo protocol ([ capsudo_proto](https://docs.rs/capsudo-proto/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capsudo_proto/index.html)) is spoken over

*some*channel. This crate defines the

[and](https://docs.rs/trait.Transport.html)

`Transport`[traits that abstract that channel, plus concrete implementations.](https://docs.rs/trait.Listener.html)

`Listener``capsudo` and `capsudod` are written
against the traits alone, so the same logic runs over:- `unix`- `AF_UNIX`socket, using real- `SCM_RIGHTS`to delegate the caller’s stdio descriptors; and
- a cross-zone Edera Protect IDM channel (built into Protect itself), which
*simulates*descriptor passing by multiplexing stream data — transparently, so neither client nor daemon needs to know. [`fakeidm`] is a throwaway TCP-backed stand-in for exercising that path on one host.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use unix::`- [UnixListener](https://docs.rs/unix/struct.UnixListener.html);
- `pub use unix::`- [UnixTransport](https://docs.rs/unix/struct.UnixTransport.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [mux](https://docs.rs/mux/index.html)
- A multiplexing transport that *simulates*`SCM_RIGHTS`over any plain byte channel.
- [ownerspec](https://docs.rs/ownerspec/index.html)
- Parsing of `user[:group]`ownership specs and octal permission modes for listener sockets — the access-control knobs (`-o`/`-m`) shared by the daemons.
- [unix](https://docs.rs/unix/index.html)
- Local transport over an `AF_UNIX``SOCK_STREAM`socket.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FdSpec](https://docs.rs/struct.FdSpec.html)
- A descriptor offered to `Transport::send`
- [Peer](https://docs.rs/struct.PeerCred.html)- Cred
- Peer credentials, where the transport can establish them.
- [Received](https://docs.rs/struct.Received.html)
- A message received from a transport, together with any file descriptors that accompanied it.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [FdDir](https://docs.rs/enum.FdDir.html)
- Which way bytes flow through a delegated descriptor, from the perspective of the side that currently holds it.
- [Transport](https://docs.rs/enum.TransportError.html)- Error
- Errors produced by a `Transport``Listener`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Control](https://docs.rs/trait.ControlSender.html)- Sender
- A detached sink for fd-less control messages, usable from another task while
the owning `Transport``recv`
- [Listener](https://docs.rs/trait.Listener.html)
- Accepts inbound capsudo connections, yielding a `Transport`

# stablebond_events - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stablebond-events/3.0.7/stablebond_events/

An Anchor generated module, providing a set of structs
mirroring the structs deriving Accounts, where each field is
a Pubkey. This is useful for specifying accounts for a client.

An Anchor generated module containing the program’s set of
instructions, where each method handler in the #[program] mod is
associated with a struct defining the input arguments to the
method. These should be used directly, when one wants to serialize
Anchor instruction data, for example, when speciying
instructions on a client.

The Anchor codegen exposes a programming model where a user defines
a set of methods inside of a #[program] module in a way similar
to writing RPC request handlers. The macro then generates a bunch of
code wrapping these user defined methods into something that can be
executed on Solana.

# quanta 0.12.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/quanta/0.12.6

# quanta

**quanta** is a high-speed timing library, useful for getting the current time *very quickly*, as well as manipulating
it.

## code of conduct

**NOTE**: All conversations and contributions to this project shall adhere to the [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/metrics-rs/quanta/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

## usage

The API documentation of this library can be found at [docs.rs/quanta](https://docs.rs/quanta/).

## general features

- count CPU cycles via Time Stamp Counter (TSC). or
- get monotonic time, in nanoseconds, based on TSC (or OS fallback)
- extremely low overhead where possible
- mockable
- cross-platform
- fun, science-y name!

## platform / architecture support

For most major platforms -- Linux, Windows, and macOS -- with processors made around or after 2008, you should have no
problems using `quanta` with full TSC support. `quanta` will always fallback to the included stdlib timing facilities if
TSC support is not present. The biggest caveat to this, as evidenced in the compatibility matrix below, is that we only
support the TSC on `x86`/`x86_64` platforms.

| Platform | stdlib fallback | TSC support? | CI tests? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux (x86/x86_64) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Linux (MIPS/ARM) | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Windows (x86/x86_64) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Windows (ARM) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| macOS (x86/x86_64) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| macOS (ARM) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| iOS (ARM) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |

## performance

`quanta` sits neck-and-neck with native OS time facilities: the cost of `Clock::now` is on par `Instant::now` from the
stdlib, if not better.

## why use this over stdlib?

Beyond having a performance edge in specific situations, the ability to use mocked time makes it easier to actually test that your application is doing the right thing when time is involved.

Additionally, and as mentioned in the general features section, `quanta` provides a safe/thin wrapper over accessing the
Time Stamp Counter, which allows measuring cycle counts over short sections of code.  This can be relevant/important for
accurately measuring performance-critical sections of code.

## alternative crates

- `chrono`- based on `std::time::SystemTime`: non-monotonic reads
- focused on timezone-based "date/time" measurements, not intervals/elapsed time
- clock cannot be altered at all (no pause, no discrete updates)

- based on
- `time`- based on `std::time::SystemTime`and`std::time::Instant`:- `time::Time`/- `time::PrimitiveDateTime`use- `SystemTime`: non-monotonic reads
- `time::Instant`uses- `Instant`: monotonic reads

- focused on timezone-based "date/time" measurements, not interval/elapsed time
- clock cannot be altered at all (no pause, no discrete updates)

- based on
- `clock`- based on `std::time::SystemTime`: non-monotonic reads
- clock can be swapped (trait-based)
- no free function for acquiring time

- based on
- `clocksource`- based on TSC w/ OS fallback; non-monotonic reads
- clock cannot be altered at all (no pause, no discrete updates)
- depends on unstable `asm!`macro + feature flag to enable TSC
- no free function for acquiring time

- `pausable_clock`- based on `std::time::Instant`: monotonic reads
- clock can be paused (time can be delayed, but not discretely updated)
- no free function for acquiring time

- based on

## license

**quanta** is licensed under the MIT license. ([LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE) or [http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

# quanta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/quanta/0.12.6/target-redirect/quanta/

## Expand description

Performant cross-platform timing with goodies.

`quanta` provides a simple and fast API for measuring the current time and the duration between
events.  It does this by providing a thin layer on top of native OS timing functions, or, if
available, using the Time Stamp Counter feature found on modern CPUs.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Internally, `quanta` maintains the concept of two potential clock sources: a reference clock and
a source clock.

The reference clock is provided by the OS, and always available. It is equivalent to what is provided by the standard library in terms of the underlying system calls being made. As it uses the native timing facilities provided by the operating system, we ultimately depend on the OS itself to give us a stable and correct value.

The source clock is a potential clock source based on the [Time Stamp Counter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Stamp_Counter) feature
found on modern CPUs.  If the TSC feature is not present or is not reliable enough, `quanta`
will transparently utilize the reference clock instead.

Depending on the underlying processor(s) in the system, `quanta` will figure out the most
accurate/efficient way to calibrate the source clock to the reference clock in order to provide
measurements scaled to wall clock time.

Details on TSC support, and calibration, are detailed below.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Beyond simply taking measurements of the current time, `quanta` provides features for more
easily working with clocks, as well as being able to enhance performance further:

- `Clock`can be mocked for testing
- globally accessible “recent” time with amortized overhead

[§](https://docs.rs#mocked-time)Mocked time

For any code that uses a `Clock`, a mocked version can be substituted.  This allows for
application authors to control the time in tests, which allows simulating not only the normal
passage of time but provides the ability to warp time forwards and backwards in order to test
corner cases in logic, etc.  Creating a mocked clock can be acheived with [ Clock::mock](https://docs.rs/struct.Clock.html#method.mock), and

[contains more details on mock usage.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html)

`Mock`[§](https://docs.rs#coarsely-updated-or-recent-time)Coarsely-updated, or recent, time

`quanta` also provides a “recent” time feature, which allows a slightly-delayed version of time
to be provided to callers, trading accuracy for speed of access.  An upkeep thread is spawned,
which is responsible for taking measurements and updating the global recent time. Callers then
can access the cached value by calling `Clock::recent`.  This interface can be 4-10x faster than
directly calling `Clock::now`, even when TSC support is available.  As the upkeep thread is the
only code updating the recent time, the accuracy of the value given to callers is limited by how
often the upkeep thread updates the time, thus the trade off between accuracy and speed of
access.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

`quanta` comes with feature flags that enable convenient conversions to time types in other
popular crates, such as:

- `prost`- provides an implementation into- `Timestamp`- `prost_types`

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-support)Platform Support

At a high level, `quanta` carries support for most major operating systems out of the box:

- Windows (`QueryPerformanceCounter`
- macOS/OS X/iOS (`mach_absolute_time`
- Linux/*BSD/Solaris (`clock_gettime`

These platforms are supported in the “reference” clock sense, and support for using the Time Stamp Counter as a clocksource is more subtle, and explained below.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-support)WASM support

This library can be built for WASM targets, but in this case the resolution and accuracy of
measurements can be limited by the WASM environment. In particular, when running on the
`wasm32-unknown-unknown` target in browsers, `quanta` will use [window.performance.now](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance/now) as a
clock. This mean the accuracy is limited to milliseconds instead of the usual nanoseconds on
other targets. When running within a WASI environment (target `wasm32-wasi`), the accuracy of
the clock depends on the VM implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#tsc-support)TSC Support

Accessing the TSC requires being on the `x86_64` architecture, with access to SSE2.
Additionally, the processor must support either constant or nonstop/invariant TSC.  This ensures
that the TSC ticks at a constant rate which can be easily scaled.

A caveat is that “constant” TSC doesn’t account for all possible power states (levels of power down or sleep that a CPU can enter to save power under light load, etc) and so a constant TSC can lead to drift in measurements over time, after they’ve been scaled to reference time.

This is a limitation of the TSC mode, as well as the nature of `quanta` not being able to know,
as the OS would, when a power state transition has happened, and thus compensate with a
recalibration. Nonstop/invariant TSC does not have this limitation and is stable over long
periods of time.

Roughly speaking, the following list contains the beginning model/generation of processors where you should be able to expect having invariant TSC support:

- Intel Nehalem and newer for server-grade
- Intel Skylake and newer for desktop-grade
- VIA Centaur Nano and newer (circumstantial evidence here)
- AMD Phenom and newer

Ultimately, `quanta` will query CPUID information to determine if the processor has the required
features to use the TSC.

[§](https://docs.rs#calibration)Calibration

As the TSC doesn’t necessarily tick at reference scale – i.e. one tick isn’t always one nanosecond – we have to apply a scaling factor when converting from source to reference time scale to provide this. We acquire this scaling factor by repeatedly taking measurements from both the reference and source clocks, until we have a statistically-relevant measure of the average scaling factor. We do some additional work to convert this scaling factor into a power-of-two number that allows us to optimize the code, and thus reduce the generated instructions required to scale a TSC value.

This calibration is stored globally and reused.  However, the first `Clock` that is created in
an application will block for a small period of time as it runs this calibration loop.  The time
spent in the calibration loop is limited to 200ms overall.  In practice, `quanta` will reach a
stable calibration quickly (usually 10-20ms, if not less) and so this deadline is unlikely to be
reached.

[§](https://docs.rs#caveats)Caveats

Utilizing the TSC can be a tricky affair, and so here is a list of caveats that may or may not apply, and is in no way exhaustive:

- CPU hotplug behavior is undefined
- raw values may time warp
- measurements from the TSC may drift past or behind the comparable reference clock

Another important caveat is that `quanta` does not track time across system suspends.  Simply
put, if a time measurement (such as using [ Instant::now](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html#method.now)) is taken, and
then the system is suspended, and then another measurement is taken, the difference between
those the two would not include the time the system was in suspend.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Clock](https://docs.rs/struct.Clock.html)
- Unified clock for taking measurements.
- [Handle](https://docs.rs/struct.Handle.html)
- Handle to a running upkeep thread.
- [Instant](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html)
- A point-in-time wall-clock measurement.
- [Mock](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html)
- Controllable time source for use in tests.
- [Upkeep](https://docs.rs/struct.Upkeep.html)
- Ultra-low-overhead access to slightly-delayed time.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Errors thrown during the creation/spawning of the upkeep thread.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoNanoseconds.html)- Nanoseconds
- Type which can be converted into a nanosecond representation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_recent.html)- recent

[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ## Mocked time
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! For any code that uses a `Clock`, a mocked version can be substituted.  This allows for
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! application authors to control the time in tests, which allows simulating not only the normal
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! passage of time but provides the ability to warp time forwards and backwards in order to test
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! corner cases in logic, etc.  Creating a mocked clock can be acheived with [`Clock::mock`], and
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! [`Mock`] contains more details on mock usage.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! ## Coarsely-updated, or recent, time
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! `quanta` also provides a "recent" time feature, which allows a slightly-delayed version of time
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! to be provided to callers, trading accuracy for speed of access.  An upkeep thread is spawned,
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! which is responsible for taking measurements and updating the global recent time. Callers then
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! can access the cached value by calling `Clock::recent`.  This interface can be 4-10x faster than
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! directly calling `Clock::now`, even when TSC support is available.  As the upkeep thread is the
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! only code updating the recent time, the accuracy of the value given to callers is limited by how
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! often the upkeep thread updates the time, thus the trade off between accuracy and speed of
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! access.
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! # Feature Flags
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! `quanta` comes with feature flags that enable convenient conversions to time types in other
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! popular crates, such as:
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! - `prost` - provides an implementation into [`Timestamp`][prost_types_timestamp] from
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!   `prost_types`
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! # Platform Support
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! At a high level, `quanta` carries support for most major operating systems out of the box:
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! - Windows ([`QueryPerformanceCounter`][QueryPerformanceCounter])
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! - macOS/OS X/iOS ([`mach_absolute_time`][mach_absolute_time])
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! - Linux/*BSD/Solaris ([`clock_gettime`][clock_gettime])
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! These platforms are supported in the "reference" clock sense, and support for using the Time
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! Stamp Counter as a clocksource is more subtle, and explained below.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! ## WASM support
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! This library can be built for WASM targets, but in this case the resolution and accuracy of
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! measurements can be limited by the WASM environment. In particular, when running on the
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target in browsers, `quanta` will use [window.performance.now] as a
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! clock. This mean the accuracy is limited to milliseconds instead of the usual nanoseconds on
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! other targets. When running within a WASI environment (target `wasm32-wasi`), the accuracy of
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! the clock depends on the VM implementation.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! # TSC Support
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! Accessing the TSC requires being on the `x86_64` architecture, with access to SSE2.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! Additionally, the processor must support either constant or nonstop/invariant TSC.  This ensures
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! that the TSC ticks at a constant rate which can be easily scaled.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! A caveat is that "constant" TSC doesn't account for all possible power states (levels of power
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! down or sleep that a CPU can enter to save power under light load, etc) and so a constant TSC
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! can lead to drift in measurements over time, after they've been scaled to reference time.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! This is a limitation of the TSC mode, as well as the nature of `quanta` not being able to know,
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! as the OS would, when a power state transition has happened, and thus compensate with a
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! recalibration. Nonstop/invariant TSC does not have this limitation and is stable over long
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! periods of time.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! Roughly speaking, the following list contains the beginning model/generation of processors where
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! you should be able to expect having invariant TSC support:
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! - Intel Nehalem and newer for server-grade
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! - Intel Skylake and newer for desktop-grade
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! - VIA Centaur Nano and newer (circumstantial evidence here)
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! - AMD Phenom and newer
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! Ultimately, `quanta` will query CPUID information to determine if the processor has the required
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! features to use the TSC.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! # Calibration
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! As the TSC doesn't necessarily tick at reference scale -- i.e. one tick isn't always one
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! nanosecond -- we have to apply a scaling factor when converting from source to reference time
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! scale to provide this.  We acquire this scaling factor by repeatedly taking measurements from
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! both the reference and source clocks, until we have a statistically-relevant measure of the
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! average scaling factor.  We do some additional work to convert this scaling factor into a
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! power-of-two number that allows us to optimize the code, and thus reduce the generated
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! instructions required to scale a TSC value.
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! This calibration is stored globally and reused.  However, the first `Clock` that is created in
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! an application will block for a small period of time as it runs this calibration loop.  The time
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! spent in the calibration loop is limited to 200ms overall.  In practice, `quanta` will reach a
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! stable calibration quickly (usually 10-20ms, if not less) and so this deadline is unlikely to be
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! reached.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! # Caveats
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! Utilizing the TSC can be a tricky affair, and so here is a list of caveats that may or may not
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! apply, and is in no way exhaustive:
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! - CPU hotplug behavior is undefined
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! - raw values may time warp
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! - measurements from the TSC may drift past or behind the comparable reference clock
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! Another important caveat is that `quanta` does not track time across system suspends.  Simply
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! put, if a time measurement (such as using [`Instant::now`][crate::Instant::now]) is taken, and
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! then the system is suspended, and then another measurement is taken, the difference between
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! those the two would not include the time the system was in suspend.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! [tsc]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Stamp_Counter
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! [QueryPerformanceCounter]: https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/ms644904(v=VS.85).aspx
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! [mach_absolute_time]: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/kernel/1462446-mach_absolute_time
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! [clock_gettime]: https://linux.die.net/man/3/clock_gettime
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! [prost_types_timestamp]: https://docs.rs/prost-types/0.7.0/prost_types/struct.Timestamp.html
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! [window.performance.now]: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance/now

[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)// Run 500 rounds of calibration before we start actually seeing what the numbers look like.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)const MINIMUM_CAL_ROUNDS: u64 = 500;
[177](https://docs.rs#177)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)// We want our maximum error to be 10 nanoseconds.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)const MAXIMUM_CAL_ERROR_NS: u64 = 10;
[180](https://docs.rs#180)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)// Don't run the calibration loop for longer than 200ms of wall time.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)const MAXIMUM_CAL_TIME_NS: u64 = 200 * 1000 * 1000;
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)#[derive(Debug)]
[185](https://docs.rs#185)enum ClockType {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    Monotonic(Monotonic),
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    Counter(Monotonic, Counter, Calibration),
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    Mock(Arc<Mock>),
[189](https://docs.rs#189)}
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
[192](https://docs.rs#192)pub(crate) struct Calibration {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    ref_time: u64,
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    src_time: u64,
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    scale_factor: u64,
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    scale_shift: u32,
[197](https://docs.rs#197)}
[198](https://docs.rs#198)
[199](https://docs.rs#199)impl Calibration {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    fn new() -> Calibration {
[201](https://docs.rs#201)        Calibration {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)            ref_time: 0,
[203](https://docs.rs#203)            src_time: 0,
[204](https://docs.rs#204)            scale_factor: 1,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)            scale_shift: 0,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)        }
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    fn reset_timebases(&mut self, reference: Monotonic, source: &Counter) {
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        self.ref_time = reference.now();
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        self.src_time = source.now();
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    fn scale_src_to_ref(&self, src_raw: u64) -> u64 {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        let delta = src_raw.saturating_sub(self.src_time);
[216](https://docs.rs#216)        let scaled = mul_div_po2_u64(delta, self.scale_factor, self.scale_shift);
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        scaled + self.ref_time
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    }
[219](https://docs.rs#219)
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    fn calibrate(&mut self, reference: Monotonic, source: &Counter) {
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        let mut variance = Variance::default();
[222](https://docs.rs#222)        let deadline = reference.now() + MAXIMUM_CAL_TIME_NS;
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)        self.reset_timebases(reference, source);
[225](https://docs.rs#225)
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        // Each busy loop should spin for 1 microsecond. (1000 nanoseconds)
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        let loop_delta = 1000;
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        loop {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)            // Busy loop to burn some time.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)            let mut last = reference.now();
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            let target = last + loop_delta;
[232](https://docs.rs#232)            while last < target {
[233](https://docs.rs#233)                last = reference.now();
[234](https://docs.rs#234)            }
[235](https://docs.rs#235)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)            // We put an upper bound on how long we run calibration before to provide a predictable
[237](https://docs.rs#237)            // overhead to the calibration process.  In practice, even if we hit the calibration
[238](https://docs.rs#238)            // deadline, we should still have run a sufficient number of rounds to get an accurate
[239](https://docs.rs#239)            // calibration.
[240](https://docs.rs#240)            if last >= deadline {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)                break;
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)
[244](https://docs.rs#244)            // Adjust our calibration before we take our measurement.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)            self.adjust_cal_ratio(reference, source);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)            let r_time = reference.now();
[248](https://docs.rs#248)            let s_raw = source.now();
[249](https://docs.rs#249)            let s_time = self.scale_src_to_ref(s_raw);
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            variance.add(s_time as f64 - r_time as f64);
[251](https://docs.rs#251)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)            // If we've collected enough samples, check what the mean and mean error are.  If we're
[253](https://docs.rs#253)            // already within the target bounds, we can break out of the calibration loop early.
[254](https://docs.rs#254)            if variance.has_significant_result() {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)                let mean = variance.mean().abs();
[256](https://docs.rs#256)                let mean_error = variance.mean_error().abs();
[257](https://docs.rs#257)                let mwe = variance.mean_with_error();
[258](https://docs.rs#258)                let samples = variance.samples();
[259](https://docs.rs#259)
[260](https://docs.rs#260)                if samples > MINIMUM_CAL_ROUNDS
[261](https://docs.rs#261)                    && mwe < MAXIMUM_CAL_ERROR_NS as f64
[262](https://docs.rs#262)                    && mean_error <= mean
[263](https://docs.rs#263)                {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)                    break;
[265](https://docs.rs#265)                }
[266](https://docs.rs#266)            }
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        }
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    fn adjust_cal_ratio(&mut self, reference: Monotonic, source: &Counter) {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        // Overall algorithm: measure the delta between our ref/src_time values and "now" versions
[272](https://docs.rs#272)        // of them, calculate the ratio between the deltas, and then find a numerator and
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        // denominator to express that ratio such that the denominator is always a power of two.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)        //
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        // In practice, this means we take the "source" delta, and find the next biggest number that
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        // is a power of two.  We then figure out the ratio that describes the difference between
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        // _those_ two values, and multiple the "reference" delta by that much, which becomes our
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        // numerator while the power-of-two "source" delta becomes our denominator.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        //
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        // Then, conversion from a raw value simply becomes a multiply and a bit shift instead of a
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        // multiply and full-blown divide.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        let ref_end = reference.now();
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        let src_end = source.now();
[284](https://docs.rs#284)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        let ref_d = ref_end.wrapping_sub(self.ref_time);
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        let src_d = src_end.wrapping_sub(self.src_time);
[287](https://docs.rs#287)
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        let src_d_po2 = src_d
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            .checked_next_power_of_two()
[290](https://docs.rs#290)            .unwrap_or_else(|| 2_u64.pow(63));
[291](https://docs.rs#291)
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        // TODO: lossy conversion back and forth just to get an approximate value, can we do better
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        // with integer math? not sure
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        let po2_ratio = src_d_po2 as f64 / src_d as f64;
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        self.scale_factor = (ref_d as f64 * po2_ratio) as u64;
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        self.scale_shift = src_d_po2.trailing_zeros();
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    }
[298](https://docs.rs#298)}
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)impl Default for Calibration {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    fn default() -> Self {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        Self::new()
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    }
[304](https://docs.rs#304)}
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)/// Unified clock for taking measurements.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
[308](https://docs.rs#308)pub struct Clock {
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    inner: ClockType,
[310](https://docs.rs#310)}
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)impl Clock {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// Creates a new clock with the optimal reference and source clocks.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    ///
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// Support for TSC, etc, are checked at the time of creation, not compile-time.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    pub fn new() -> Clock {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        let reference = Monotonic::default();
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        let inner = if detection::has_counter_support() {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)            let source = Counter;
[320](https://docs.rs#320)            let calibration = GLOBAL_CALIBRATION.get_or_init(|| {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)                let mut calibration = Calibration::new();
[322](https://docs.rs#322)                calibration.calibrate(reference, &source);
[323](https://docs.rs#323)                calibration
[324](https://docs.rs#324)            });
[325](https://docs.rs#325)            ClockType::Counter(reference, source, *calibration)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        } else {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)            ClockType::Monotonic(reference)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)        };
[329](https://docs.rs#329)
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        Clock { inner }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// Creates a new clock that is mocked for controlling the underlying time.
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    ///
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// Returns a [`Clock`] instance and a handle to the underlying [`Mock`] source so that the
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    /// caller can control the passage of time.
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    pub fn mock() -> (Clock, Arc<Mock>) {
[338](https://docs.rs#338)        let mock = Arc::new(Mock::new());
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        let clock = Clock {
[340](https://docs.rs#340)            inner: ClockType::Mock(mock.clone()),
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        };
[342](https://docs.rs#342)
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        (clock, mock)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    }
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    /// Gets the current time, scaled to reference time.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    ///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    /// This method is the spiritual equivalent of [`std::time::Instant::now`].  It is guaranteed
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// to return a monotonically increasing value between calls to the same `Clock` instance.
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    ///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// Returns an [`Instant`].
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    pub fn now(&self) -> Instant {
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        match &self.inner {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            ClockType::Monotonic(monotonic) => Instant(monotonic.now()),
[355](https://docs.rs#355)            ClockType::Counter(_, counter, _) => self.scaled(counter.now()),
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            ClockType::Mock(mock) => Instant(mock.value()),
[357](https://docs.rs#357)        }
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    }
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// Gets the underlying time from the fastest available clock source.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    ///
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    /// As the clock source may or may not be the TSC, value is not guaranteed to be in nanoseconds
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// or to be monotonic.  Value can be scaled to reference time by calling either [`scaled`]
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// or [`delta`].
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// [`scaled`]: Clock::scaled
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// [`delta`]: Clock::delta
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    pub fn raw(&self) -> u64 {
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        match &self.inner {
[370](https://docs.rs#370)            ClockType::Monotonic(monotonic) => monotonic.now(),
[371](https://docs.rs#371)            ClockType::Counter(_, counter, _) => counter.now(),
[372](https://docs.rs#372)            ClockType::Mock(mock) => mock.value(),
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        }
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    }
[375](https://docs.rs#375)
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// Scales a raw measurement to reference time.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    ///
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// You must scale raw measurements to ensure your result is in nanoseconds.  The raw
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// measurement is not guaranteed to be in nanoseconds and may vary.  It is only OK to avoid
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// scaling raw measurements if you don't need actual nanoseconds.
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    ///
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// Returns an [`Instant`].
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    pub fn scaled(&self, value: u64) -> Instant {
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        let scaled = match &self.inner {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)            ClockType::Counter(_, _, calibration) => calibration.scale_src_to_ref(value),
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            _ => value,
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        };
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        Instant(scaled)
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// Calculates the delta, in nanoseconds, between two raw measurements.
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    ///
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// This method is very similar to [`delta`] but reduces overhead
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// for high-frequency measurements that work with nanosecond
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// counts internally, as it avoids the conversion of the delta
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// into [`Duration`].
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// [`delta`]: Clock::delta
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    pub fn delta_as_nanos(&self, start: u64, end: u64) -> u64 {
[401](https://docs.rs#401)        // Safety: we want wrapping_sub on the end/start delta calculation so that two measurements
[402](https://docs.rs#402)        // split across a rollover boundary still return the right result.  However, we also know
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        // the TSC could potentially give us different values between cores/sockets, so we're just
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        // doing our due diligence here to make sure we're not about to create some wacky duration.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        if end <= start {
[406](https://docs.rs#406)            return 0;
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        }
[408](https://docs.rs#408)
[409](https://docs.rs#409)        let delta = end.wrapping_sub(start);
[410](https://docs.rs#410)        match &self.inner {
[411](https://docs.rs#411)            ClockType::Counter(_, _, calibration) => {
[412](https://docs.rs#412)                mul_div_po2_u64(delta, calibration.scale_factor, calibration.scale_shift)
[413](https://docs.rs#413)            }
[414](https://docs.rs#414)            _ => delta,
[415](https://docs.rs#415)        }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// Calculates the delta between two raw measurements.
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    ///
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// This method is slightly faster when you know you need the delta between two raw
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// measurements, or a start/end measurement, than using [`scaled`] for both conversions.
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// In code that simply needs access to the whole number of nanoseconds
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// between the two measurements, consider [`Clock::delta_as_nanos`]
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// instead, which is slightly faster than having to call both this method
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// and [`Duration::as_nanos`].
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// [`scaled`]: Clock::scaled
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// [`delta_as_nanos`]: Clock::delta_as_nanos
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    pub fn delta(&self, start: u64, end: u64) -> Duration {
[431](https://docs.rs#431)        Duration::from_nanos(self.delta_as_nanos(start, end))
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    }

[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// Gets the most recent current time, scaled to reference time.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    ///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// This method provides ultra-low-overhead access to a slightly-delayed version of the current
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// time.  Instead of querying the underlying source clock directly, a shared, global value is
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// read directly without the need to scale to reference time.

[442](https://docs.rs#442)    /// well as the details of the "current time" mechanism.
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    ///
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    /// If the upkeep thread has not been started, the return value will be `0`.
[445](https://docs.rs#445)    ///
[446](https://docs.rs#446)    /// Returns an [`Instant`].
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    pub fn recent(&self) -> Instant {

[449](https://docs.rs#449)            ClockType::Mock(mock) => Instant(mock.value()),
[450](https://docs.rs#450)            _ => Instant(GLOBAL_RECENT.load()),
[451](https://docs.rs#451)        }

[517](https://docs.rs#517)#[inline]
[518](https://docs.rs#518)pub(crate) fn get_recent() -> Instant {
[519](https://docs.rs#519)    // We make a small trade-off here where if the global recent time isn't zero, we use that,
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    // regardless of whether or not there's a thread-specific clock override.  Otherwise, we would
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    // blow our performance budget.
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    //
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    // Given that global recent time shouldn't ever be getting _actually_ updated in tests, this
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    // should be a reasonable trade-off.
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    let recent = GLOBAL_RECENT.load();
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    if recent == 0 {
[527](https://docs.rs#527)        get_now()
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    } else {
[529](https://docs.rs#529)        Instant(recent)
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    }

[533](https://docs.rs#533)#[inline]
[534](https://docs.rs#534)fn mul_div_po2_u64(value: u64, numer: u64, denom: u32) -> u64 {
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    // Modified muldiv routine where the denominator has to be a power of two. `denom` is expected
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    // to be the number of bits to shift, not the actual decimal value.
[537](https://docs.rs#537)    let mut v = u128::from(value);
[538](https://docs.rs#538)    v *= u128::from(numer);
[539](https://docs.rs#539)    v >>= denom;
[540](https://docs.rs#540)    v as u64

[602](https://docs.rs#602)    #[cfg_attr(not(feature = "flaky_tests"), ignore)]
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    fn test_reference_source_calibration() {
[604](https://docs.rs#604)        let mut clock = Clock::new();
[605](https://docs.rs#605)        let reference = Monotonic::default();
[606](https://docs.rs#606)
[607](https://docs.rs#607)        let loops = 10000;
[608](https://docs.rs#608)
[609](https://docs.rs#609)        let mut overall = Variance::new();
[610](https://docs.rs#610)        let mut src_samples = [0u64; 1024];
[611](https://docs.rs#611)        let mut ref_samples = [0u64; 1024];
[612](https://docs.rs#612)
[613](https://docs.rs#613)        for _ in 0..loops {
[614](https://docs.rs#614)            // We have to reset the "timebase" of the clock/calibration when testing in this way.
[615](https://docs.rs#615)            //
[616](https://docs.rs#616)            // Since `quanta` is designed around mimicing `Instant`, we care about measuring the _passage_ of time, but
[617](https://docs.rs#617)            // not matching our calculation of wall-clock time to the system's calculation of wall-clock time, in terms
[618](https://docs.rs#618)            // of their absolute values.
[619](https://docs.rs#619)            //
[620](https://docs.rs#620)            // As the system adjusts its clocks over time, whether due to NTP skew, or delays in updating the derived
[621](https://docs.rs#621)            // monotonic time, and so on, our original measurement base from the reference source -- which we use to
[622](https://docs.rs#622)            // anchor how we convert our scaled source measurement into the same reference timebase -- can skew further
[623](https://docs.rs#623)            // away from the current reference time in terms of the rate at which it ticks forward.
[624](https://docs.rs#624)            //
[625](https://docs.rs#625)            // Essentially, what we're saying here is that we want to test the scaling ratio that we generated in
[626](https://docs.rs#626)            // calibration, but not necessarily that the resulting value -- which is meant to be in the same timebase as
[627](https://docs.rs#627)            // the reference -- is locked to the reference itself. For example, if the reference is in nanoseconds, we
[628](https://docs.rs#628)            // want our source to be scaled to nanoseconds, too. We don't care if the system shoves the reference back
[629](https://docs.rs#629)            // and forth via NTP skew, etc... we just need to do enough source-to-reference calibration loops to figure
[630](https://docs.rs#630)            // out what the right amount is to scale the TSC -- since we require an invariant/nonstop TSC -- to get it
[631](https://docs.rs#631)            // to nanoseconds.
[632](https://docs.rs#632)            //
[633](https://docs.rs#633)            // At the risk of saying _too much_, while the delta between `Clock::now` and `Monotonic::now` may grow over
[634](https://docs.rs#634)            // time if the timebases are not reset, we can readily observe in this test that the delta between the
[635](https://docs.rs#635)            // first/last measurement loop for both source/reference are independently close i.e. the ratio by which we
[636](https://docs.rs#636)            // scale the source measurements gets it close, and stays close, to the reference measurements in terms of
[637](https://docs.rs#637)            // the _passage_ of time.
[638](https://docs.rs#638)            clock.reset_timebase();
[639](https://docs.rs#639)
[640](https://docs.rs#640)            for i in 0..1024 {
[641](https://docs.rs#641)                src_samples[i] = clock.now().0;
[642](https://docs.rs#642)                ref_samples[i] = reference.now();
[643](https://docs.rs#643)            }
[644](https://docs.rs#644)
[645](https://docs.rs#645)            let is_src_monotonic = src_samples
[646](https://docs.rs#646)                .iter()
[647](https://docs.rs#647)                .map(Some)
[648](https://docs.rs#648)                .reduce(|last, current| last.and_then(|lv| current.filter(|cv| *cv >= lv)))
[649](https://docs.rs#649)                .flatten()
[650](https://docs.rs#650)                .copied();
[651](https://docs.rs#651)            assert_eq!(is_src_monotonic, Some(src_samples[1023]));
[652](https://docs.rs#652)
[653](https://docs.rs#653)            let is_ref_monotonic = ref_samples
[654](https://docs.rs#654)                .iter()
[655](https://docs.rs#655)                .map(Some)
[656](https://docs.rs#656)                .reduce(|last, current| last.and_then(|lv| current.filter(|cv| *cv >= lv)))
[657](https://docs.rs#657)                .flatten()
[658](https://docs.rs#658)                .copied();
[659](https://docs.rs#659)            assert_eq!(is_ref_monotonic, Some(ref_samples[1023]));
[660](https://docs.rs#660)
[661](https://docs.rs#661)            let local = src_samples
[662](https://docs.rs#662)                .iter()
[663](https://docs.rs#663)                .zip(ref_samples.iter())
[664](https://docs.rs#664)                .map(|(s, r)| *s as f64 - *r as f64)
[665](https://docs.rs#665)                .map(|f| f.abs())
[666](https://docs.rs#666)                .collect::<Variance>();
[667](https://docs.rs#667)
[668](https://docs.rs#668)            overall.merge(&local);
[669](https://docs.rs#669)        }
[670](https://docs.rs#670)
[671](https://docs.rs#671)        println!(
[672](https://docs.rs#672)            "reference/source delta: mean={} error={} mean-var={} samples={}",
[673](https://docs.rs#673)            overall.mean(),
[674](https://docs.rs#674)            overall.error(),
[675](https://docs.rs#675)            overall.variance_of_mean(),
[676](https://docs.rs#676)            overall.len(),
[677](https://docs.rs#677)        );
[678](https://docs.rs#678)
[679](https://docs.rs#679)        // If things are out of sync more than 1000ns, something is likely scaled wrong.
[680](https://docs.rs#680)        assert!(overall.mean() < 1000.0);
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    }
[682](https://docs.rs#682)
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    #[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    #[test]
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    #[cfg_attr(not(feature = "flaky_tests"), ignore)]
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    fn measure_source_reference_self_timing() {
[687](https://docs.rs#687)        let source = Counter::default();
[688](https://docs.rs#688)        let reference = Monotonic::default();
[689](https://docs.rs#689)
[690](https://docs.rs#690)        let loops = 10000;
[691](https://docs.rs#691)
[692](https://docs.rs#692)        let mut src_deltas = Vec::new();
[693](https://docs.rs#693)        let mut src_samples = [0u64; 100];
[694](https://docs.rs#694)
[695](https://docs.rs#695)        for _ in 0..loops {
[696](https://docs.rs#696)            let start = Instant::now();
[697](https://docs.rs#697)            for i in 0..100 {
[698](https://docs.rs#698)                src_samples[i] = source.now();
[699](https://docs.rs#699)            }
[700](https://docs.rs#700)
[701](https://docs.rs#701)            src_deltas.push(start.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
[702](https://docs.rs#702)        }
[703](https://docs.rs#703)
[704](https://docs.rs#704)        let mut ref_deltas = Vec::new();
[705](https://docs.rs#705)        let mut ref_samples = [0u64; 100];
[706](https://docs.rs#706)
[707](https://docs.rs#707)        for _ in 0..loops {
[708](https://docs.rs#708)            let start = Instant::now();
[709](https://docs.rs#709)            for i in 0..100 {
[710](https://docs.rs#710)                ref_samples[i] = reference.now();
[711](https://docs.rs#711)            }
[712](https://docs.rs#712)
[713](https://docs.rs#713)            ref_deltas.push(start.elapsed().as_secs_f64());
[714](https://docs.rs#714)        }
[715](https://docs.rs#715)
[716](https://docs.rs#716)        let src_variance = src_deltas.into_iter().collect::<Variance>();
[717](https://docs.rs#717)        let ref_variance = ref_deltas.into_iter().collect::<Variance>();
[718](https://docs.rs#718)
[719](https://docs.rs#719)        let src_variance_ns = Duration::from_secs_f64(src_variance.mean() / 100.0);
[720](https://docs.rs#720)        let ref_variance_ns = Duration::from_secs_f64(ref_variance.mean() / 100.0);
[721](https://docs.rs#721)
[722](https://docs.rs#722)        println!(
[723](https://docs.rs#723)            "source call average: {:?}, reference call average: {:?}",
[724](https://docs.rs#724)            src_variance_ns, ref_variance_ns
[725](https://docs.rs#725)        );
[726](https://docs.rs#726)    }

# Clock in quanta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quanta/0.12.6/quanta/struct.Clock.html

`pub struct Clock { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Unified clock for taking measurements.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new clock with the optimal reference and source clocks.

Support for TSC, etc, are checked at the time of creation, not compile-time.

Gets the current time, scaled to reference time.

This method is the spiritual equivalent of [ std::time::Instant::now](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/time/struct.Instant.html#method.now).  It is guaranteed
to return a monotonically increasing value between calls to the same

`Clock` instance.Returns an [ Instant](https://docs.rs/struct.Instant.html).

Scales a raw measurement to reference time.

# Upkeep in quanta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quanta/0.12.6/quanta/struct.Upkeep.html

`pub struct Upkeep { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Ultra-low-overhead access to slightly-delayed time.

In some applications, there can be a need to check the current time very often, so much so that the overhead of checking the time can begin to eat up measurable overhead. For some of these cases, the time may need to be accessed often but does not necessarily need to be incredibly accurate: one millisecond granularity could be entirely acceptable.

For these cases, we provide a slightly-delayed version of the time to callers via
[ Clock::recent](https://docs.rs/struct.Clock.html#method.recent), which is updated by a background upkeep thread.  That thread is configured
and spanwed via

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Upkeep.html)

`Upkeep`[ Upkeep](https://docs.rs/struct.Upkeep.html) can construct a new clock (or be passed an existing clock to use), and given an
update interval, and it will faithfully attempt to update the global recent time on the
specified interval.  There is a trade-off to be struck in terms of how often the time is
updated versus the required accuracy.  Checking the time and updating the global reference is
itself not zero-cost, and so care must be taken to analyze the number of readers in order to
ensure that, given a particular update interval, the upkeep thread is saving more CPU time than
would be spent otherwise by directly querying the current time.

The recent time is read and written atomically.  It is global to an application, so if another
codepath creates the upkeep thread, the interval chosen by that instantiation will be the one
that all callers of [ Clock::recent](https://docs.rs/struct.Clock.html#method.recent) end up using.

Multiple upkeep threads cannot exist at the same time. A new upkeep thread can be started if the old one is dropped and returns.

In terms of performance, reading the recent time can be up to two to three times as fast as reading the current time in the optimized case of using the Time Stamp Counter source. In practice, while a caller might expect to take 12-14ns to read the TSC and scale it to reference time, the recent time can be read in 4-5ns, with no reference scale conversion required.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new [ Upkeep](https://docs.rs/struct.Upkeep.html).

This creates a new internal clock for acquiring the current time.  If you have an existing
[ Clock](https://docs.rs/struct.Clock.html) that is already calibrated, it is slightly faster to clone it and construct the
builder with

[to avoid recalibrating.](https://docs.rs/struct.Upkeep.html#method.new_with_clock)

`new_with_clock`Start the upkeep thread, periodically updating the global coarse time.

[ Handle](https://docs.rs/struct.Handle.html) represents a drop guard for the upkeep thread if it is successfully spawned.
Dropping the handle will also instruct the upkeep thread to stop and exist, so the handle
must be held while the upkeep thread should continue to run.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If either an existing upkeep thread is running, or there was an issue when attempting to spawn the upkeep thread, an error variant will be returned describing the error.
